links.note: 601 calls the family a lamp that does not dwindle (குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம்) which dies when the grime of sloth spreads over it (மடியென்னும் மாசூர). 753 calls wealth a lamp that does not fail (பொருளென்னும் பொய்யா விளக்கம்) which goes where its owner intends and cuts the darkness. The same 'X என்னும் ... விளக்கம்' figure is used twice in the Book of Wealth, and Parimelazhagar glosses both as a நந்தா விளக்கு; one lamp is shown dispelling darkness abroad, the other being put out from within.

601 has the lamp of family smothered by sloth; 299 says that for the worthy the only lamp is the unfailing one (பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு), which Parimelazhagar takes as not-lying, the lamp against inner darkness. Both make an inherited or inward good into a lamp, but 601's 'undwindling' lamp can still go out (மாய்ந்து கெடும்), so the epithet குன்றா describes the lineage only while its members keep it clean.

602 tells those who want their family to be a family (குடியைக் குடியாக வேண்டுபவர்) to live treating sloth as sloth, or killing it (மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல்). 1028 says those who build the family have no season to wait for, and that if they idle and think of their dignity it is ruined (மடிசெய்து மானங் கருதக் கெடும்). 1028 gives 602's rule its practical form: for the family-builder sloth shows up as waiting for the right time and standing on dignity.

602 states the negative condition for a family's standing: remove sloth. 1022 states the positive one: the family lengthens (நீளும் குடி) through long work in two things, effort and mature knowledge (ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும்). Read together, absence of sloth is necessary but 1022 adds knowledge beside effort.

no_link_reason: Its claim that the sloth-carrier's family dies before he does (குடிமடியும் தன்னினும் முந்து) is restated by its chapter neighbours; I found no verse outside the chapter that adds to it beyond the shared topic.

links.note: 604: for those sunk in sloth, without excellent effort, the family dies and faults multiply (குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும்). 171: if one covets others' goods without fairness, the family perishes and faults come at once (குடிபொன்றிக் குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்). The same double consequence, ruin of the line plus growth of fault, is attached to a vice of omission in one book and a vice of grasping in the other.

605 lists delay, forgetting, sloth and sleep as the craft that those of a ruin-bound nature desire (கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்). 920 lists double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has cast off (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு). Both verses give a short catalogue and tie it to people already marked for ruin, leaving open whether the listed things cause the ruin or are its sign.

605 makes four habits a boat (கலன்) that the ruin-bound love to board; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read it as a vessel that drops its passengers mid-sea, though Parimelazhagar notes others read கலன் as an ornament. 1068 makes begging an unsafe boat (ஏமாப்பில் தோணி) that splits on the rock of refusal. In both a way of living is a vessel trusted by the person in it and bound to fail him.

605 treats sloth and its companions as something the ruin-bound choose and desire (காமக் கலன்). 371 says sloth itself arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 371 puts a cause behind what 605 describes as a preference, which matches 605's own word கெடுநீரார், people whose nature is already to perish.

606: even when the holdings of those who own the earth come to them (படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும்), the slothful rarely reach an excellent fruit. 591: what makes one 'a possessor' is energy; do those without it possess even what they possess (உடையது உடையரோ)? Both deny that having things amounts to benefiting from them when the inner quality is missing. Parimelazhagar notes another reading of 606 in which the earth-owners' support, not their wealth, is what comes.

606 says the greatest possessions yield the slothful no excellent fruit (மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது). 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with those who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). The two share the 'ஆகியக் கண்ணும் / அமைந்தக் கண்ணும்' concession: resources do not work without the action of those who hold them.

607 says those who love sloth and make no excellent effort will hear rebuke and then scorn (இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளுஞ் சொல் கேட்பர்). 784 says friendship exists so that one may go ahead and rebuke a friend who oversteps (மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). Parimelazhagar reads 607's இடி as exactly this rebuke by friends, which fails and turns into contempt; on that reading 607 shows the limit of the remedy 784 describes.

607: the slothful end up hearing words of scorn (எள்ளுஞ் சொல்). 1040: seeing those who sit idle saying 'we have nothing', the good woman called Land laughs (நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்). Both give idleness the same penalty, being laughed at, once from people and once from the personified earth.

608: if sloth lodges in one of family standing it puts him into slavery to his enemies (அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்). 616: absence of effort puts one into want (இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). The identical closing phrase makes sloth an agent that ushers a person into a condition; the neighbouring chapters thus name two destinations, poverty and subjection, and Parimelazhagar links them in his note on 616, where want leads to destruction by enemies.

609: when a man ends the rule of sloth over him (மடியாண்மை மாற்ற), the fault that came into his குடியாண்மை is gone; Parimelazhagar splits the word into family and manhood, Manakkudavar reads it as the management of the family. 1026 says good manhood is making the management of the house one was born in one's own (நல்லாண்மை ... இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்). 1026 supports reading the two terms of 609 together: manhood is measured in the household, and sloth is what unseats it.

604 says that for the slothful the family dies and faults multiply (குற்றம் பெருகும்). 609 says the fault is destroyed (குற்றம் ... கெடும்) once a man changes his sloth. 609 makes 604's decline reversible; Parimelazhagar goes further and takes 609's faults to include ones that arose from other causes.

610: a king without sloth obtains at once all that the one who measured with his foot strode over (அடியளந்தான் தாஅய தெல்லாம்). 484: even if one aims at the world it comes to hand, if one acts with the time and by the place (ஞாலம் கருதினுங் கைகூடும்). Both promise the whole earth to a ruler on a condition, and the conditions differ: unbroken exertion in one, waiting on time and place in the other.

610 gives the unslothful king the whole measured world. 606, in the same chapter, says that even when the wealth of earth-owners arrives the slothful get no excellent fruit from it. Together they separate two things: sloth does not only block gaining the world, it also empties the world of value when it is handed over.

611: do not flag saying 'it is hard' (அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை), for effort will give the greatness (பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்). 26: those who do what is hard to do are great, those who cannot are small (செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர்). 26 defines greatness by hard deeds as if it were a fixed difference between people; 611 says the greatness needed is itself produced by trying.

611 answers the thought 'this is hard' with effort. 537 says nothing is impossible on the ground of being hard (அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லை) if done with the tool of unforgetting care (பொச்சாவாக் கருவியால்). The same objection is met in two chapters with two different instruments, exertion and vigilance.

612: guard against the work failing in the doing, because the world has left those who left the work's need undone (வினைக்குறை தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு), on Parimelazhagar's reading; Manakkudavar takes the second line the other way, that the world does not leave those who finish. 670: whatever other firmness they have, the world does not want those who do not want firmness in action (வேண்டாரை வேண்டாது உலகு). Both make the world's regard answer in kind to how a person treats the task.

612 warns against abandoning a task midway (வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல்). 674 says the remainder of a task, like the remainder of an enmity, burns like the remainder of a fire (தீயெச்சம் போலத் தெறும்). 674 supplies a reason 612 does not give: the unfinished part is not inert but goes on doing damage.

613: the distinction called helping others rests in the quality called effort (தாளாண்மை ... வேளாண்மை). 212: all the wealth brought in by exertion is for doing help to the deserving (தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம் தக்கார்க்கு வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு). The same pair of words, தாள் and வேளாண்மை, is joined in the Book of Virtue as purpose and in the Book of Wealth as precondition: effort exists for giving, and giving depends on effort.

613 calls generosity a pride (செருக்கு) that stays only with effort. 598 says those without inner drive do not reach the pride of saying 'we have been generous' (வள்ளியம் என்னுஞ் செருக்கு). Both use செருக்கு approvingly for the giver's satisfaction and both make it unavailable to the inert; one names the missing thing as drive, the other as labour.

613 says the standing of a benefactor rests on labour. 1035 says those whose way is to eat what their hands produce do not beg and give to those who beg without hiding anything (கைசெய்தூண் மாலையவர்). The farming chapter shows 613's general claim in one occupation: the person who works with his hands is the one in a position to give.

614: the helpfulness of one without effort fails like a sword being wielded in the hand of a பேடி (பேடிகை வாளாண்மை). 727: the treatise learned by one who fears the assembly is a bright sword in the hand of a பேடி among enemies (பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள்). The same figure is used for two unused capacities, the will to give without the labour that funds it, and learning without the nerve to speak; Parimelazhagar explains 614 as fear making the sword useless, as poverty makes the intention useless.

614 says the generosity of a man without effort comes to nothing. 219 says that for a man of good feeling, being poor just is not being able to do the helpful things he would do (செயும்நீர செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு). 219 shows the same blocked intention from the inside and without blame, so 614's scorn falls only on the case where the lack of means comes from not working.

615: one who does not want pleasure and wants the work (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) is a pillar that wipes away his kin's sorrow and holds them up. 628: one who does not want pleasure (இன்பம் விழையான்) and calls hardship natural does not come to sorrow. The same opening phrase carries two results in adjoining chapters: not seeking pleasure spares the man himself in 628 and, joined to love of work, relieves others in 615.

615 makes the work-loving man a pillar that props his kin (துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்). 1030 says a family with no good person to stand by and prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. 1030 states the cost of the absence of the figure 615 praises, with the same verb ஊன்று.

615 praises the one who wants the work (வினைவிழைவான்) and not pleasure. 901 says those who desire the wife do not reach the excellent fruit, and that this is the very thing those who desire action do not want (வினைவிழையார் வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது). Both set the desire for action against a desire for enjoyment and use nearly the same word for the man of action.

616: effort makes fortune (முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும்) and lack of effort brings one into want. 371: unflagging effort arises from a fate of gain, and sloth from a fate of loss (ஆகூழால் தோன்றும் அசைவின்மை ... போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). 616 makes effort the cause of wealth; 371 makes fate the cause of effort, so on 371's account the causal chain in 616 starts one step earlier and is not in the person's hands.

616 says effort produces fortune. 594 says increase asks the way and goes to the one of unwavering drive (அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா ஊக்கமுடையானுழை). Both place the source of prosperity in the person's exertion, and 594 pictures it as prosperity doing the seeking. The first word of 594 is truncated in this edition (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்).

617: they say the dark Mugadi lives in sloth and the lotus goddess lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி ... தாளுளாள் தாமரையினாள்). 167: the fair goddess, grudging the envious man, shows him to her elder sister (செய்யவள் தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). Both use the paired sisters of fortune and misfortune, and each names a different trait that decides which sister a person gets: envy in the Book of Virtue, sloth in the Book of Wealth.

617 houses Mugadi in a man's sloth. 936 says those covered by the Mugadi called gambling (சூதென்னும் முகடியான் மூடப்பட்டார்) do not fill their bellies and suffer. The rare name முகடி appears in both; in 617 she resides in a habit, in 936 a habit is itself called by her name.

617 says the lotus goddess dwells in the effort of the man without sloth (தாளுளாள்). 84 says the fair goddess dwells gladly in the house of one who tends good guests with a glad face (செய்யாள் உறையும்). Both say where Fortune lives, and the addresses differ: a person's labour in one, a hospitable home in the other.

618: lacking good fortune is no blame to anyone; knowing what should be known and not exerting oneself is the blame (பொறியின்மை யார்க்கும் பழியன்று ... ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி). 371 says sloth itself arises from a fate of loss (போகூழால் தோன்றும் மடி). If 371 is read as saying fate causes a person's lack of effort, then the lack of effort 618 blames is a case of the ill fortune 618 excuses; the conflict depends on that causal reading of 371.

618 separates what is no disgrace (having no luck) from what is (not working). 988 says want is no disgrace to a person who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று). Both refuse to count an outward lack as shame and move the test to something in the person, effort in one and character in the other.

619: even if a thing cannot come about through the divine (தெய்வத்தான் ஆகாதெனினும்), effort gives the wage of the body's toil. 1023: for one who says 'I will build up my family', the divine girds its cloth and goes ahead of him (தெய்வம் மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந்துறும்). 619 treats தெய்வம் as a possible obstacle that effort partly outlasts; 1023 treats it as an ally that effort enlists, so the two give different pictures of how the same power stands to the one who works.

619 promises effort a return equal to the labour (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி) even against the divine order. 377 says that even those who have amassed crores can enjoy them only in the way the apportioner has apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகையல்லால் ... துய்த்தல் அரிது). 377 limits what 619 leaves open: the wage may be earned and still not be enjoyed.

620: those who labour on without faltering and without delay will see even fate's back (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). 380: what is stronger than fate? Even if one devises something else, it gets there first (மற்றொன்று சூழினுந் தான்முந்துறும்). Taken as general claims they conflict, one saying fate can be outlasted and the other that nothing overtakes it; Parimelazhagar softens 620 by saying fate can be turned back only by trying many times, not at once.

620 ends 'தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்', those who labour without delay, and says they see fate's back. 1024 ends with the same phrase, 'தம்குடியைத் தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர்க்கு', and says that for them the outcome arrives by itself without deliberation (சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும்). The same people are described twice, once as defeating an opposing power and once as finding the result come unsought.

620 says persistent labour gets past fate. 269 says that for those who have reached the power of austerity even leaping past Death becomes possible (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). Each takes the limit usually held to be unbeatable in its own sphere and says sustained discipline can cross it, in worldly action and in ascetic practice. The last word of 269 is misprinted in this edition (பட்டவர்க்குல்).
